rule: When an extension with a view command goes to the Store: add at least one screenshot in a metadata folder, because reviewers block a submission that has none.
When you take a metadata screenshot: use the Raycast Window Capture hotkey with Save to Metadata, because it gives the size and padding the Store expects.
When you add a metadata image: show the extension inside Raycast, not the third-party app, because the Store page must show what the extension itself does.
When you add a metadata image: use a real capture of Raycast, not a generated or mocked-up picture, because reviewers reject images that do not show the real extension.
When an extension shows private data: use mock data in the metadata screenshots instead of blurring it, because blurred images look broken and real data leaks.
When you add several metadata images: use the same background for all of them, because the Store wants one consistent visual expression.
When you capture a metadata image: make sure the local development extension icon is not in the bottom bar, because dev-only elements must not show in the Store.
When you prepare metadata images: do not add an image that only lists the commands, because the Store already shows the commands in a separate tab.
When you add metadata images: make each one show a different screen or state, because a duplicate screenshot adds nothing to the Store page.
When every command in an extension is no-view: leave out the metadata folder, because there is no Raycast view to capture.
When an image explains setup rather than the extension in use: link it from the README and keep the file in the media folder, because metadata is only for screenshots.
When you check a metadata image: make sure it is not cropped, skewed or framed by a white border, because the Store needs the full padded window.
When a command has several distinct states: add a screenshot for each important one, because more screenshots help users understand the extension.
When you make the extension icon: check that it reads well in both light and dark appearance, because reviewers reject icons with low contrast in one theme.
When the extension icon does not work in both themes: make one with icon.ray.so, because it gives Store-ready icons that read in light and dark.
When you publish an extension: replace the default Raycast icon with your own, because extensions that keep the default icon are rejected.
When you pick the extension icon: use an image that relates to what the extension does, because a generic icon makes it hard to recognize in the Store.
When you pick the extension icon: do not use the logo of a different product, because a misleading icon sets the wrong expectations.
When you add the extension icon: supply it as a PNG file, because the Store expects the extension icon in PNG format.
When you draw or export the extension icon: keep its edges and details sharp, because an upscaled or low-resolution icon looks blurry in the Store.
When the light and dark icons would be identical: keep one icon file, because a separate dark variant only adds upkeep.
When you commit an image file: open it locally first to confirm it renders, because a corrupt upload shows as a broken image.
When you change the extension icon: capture the metadata images again, because old screenshots would still show the old icon.
When an asset is no longer used: delete it from the assets folder, because the Store asks for no unused icons or images.
When an icon already exists in assets: do not commit a second copy elsewhere, because duplicate images grow the extension for nothing.
When you prepare a PR: remove dev artifacts such as scratch files, local notes or build output, because they do not belong in the extension.
When you set up .gitignore: use the standard Raycast one with node_modules, raycast-env.d.ts and the Swift and Rust build folders, because those files are generated.
When raycast-env.d.ts is generated: list it in .gitignore and do not commit it, because Raycast creates it again from the manifest.
When you write tsconfig.json: include src/**/* and raycast-env.d.ts, because the generated preference and argument types live in that file.
When you set up linting: use an ESLint 9 flat config that extends @raycast/eslint-config, because that is what the current templates ship.
When you contribute to an existing extension: keep its ESLint config file as it is, because an unrelated config change makes the PR hard to review.
When an extension uses an old API version or ESLint setup: run npx ray migrate, because it upgrades the code and config to current Raycast conventions.
When you change dependencies: run npm install and commit the matching package-lock.json, because CI installs from the lock file with npm.
When a package in package.json is not imported anywhere: remove it, because unused dependencies grow the install and the review surface.
When a package is listed in both dependencies and devDependencies: keep only one entry, because two entries let the versions drift.
When you set up package.json: do not add a package named ray as a dependency, because the ray CLI already comes with @raycast/api.
When you write package.json scripts: keep the build script as ray build, because the Store pipeline expects the Raycast build.
When you write package.json scripts: keep the template prepublishOnly guard and publish script, because they stop an accidental publish to npm.
When an extension uses macOS-only APIs such as AppleScript or MenuBarExtra: set platforms to macOS in package.json, because otherwise it installs on Windows and fails.
When the code uses only cross-platform Node APIs: do not restrict platforms to macOS, because Windows users could use the extension too.
When you set the author field: use your Raycast Store username, because validation fails for a handle that has no Raycast account.
When you contribute to an extension someone else owns: leave the author field alone and add yourself to contributors, because the author stays the owner.
When you create a new extension: do not list contributors who did not work on it, because the contributors field credits real work.
When you do not publish for an organisation: leave out the owner field, because owner makes the extension private to that team.
When you write package.json: remove manifest properties that the extension does not use, because the manifest must declare only what it needs.
When you name an extension: leave out words like raycast or extension, because every Store item is already a Raycast extension.
When you rename an extension: rename its folder to the new name as well, because the folder and the name field must agree.
When an extension has a single command: give the extension a title that says what it does, not only a brand, because users browse the Store by purpose.
When a brand name is styled in all caps: write the extension title in normal Title Case, because Store titles follow the Apple Style Guide.
When a name could be confused with an official or existing extension: make it more specific, because users must tell the extensions apart.
When you name an MCP server or AI tool: include the product it belongs to, because a generic name says nothing about its source.
When you title a command: use a verb and a noun such as Generate Avatar, because the Store naming guide asks for that form.
When a command title is vague: rename it to say exactly what the command does, because users choose commands by their titles.
When an action runs at once or opens preferences: do not end its title with an ellipsis, because the ellipsis marks an action with a submenu.
When a command renders its root view: do not set navigationTitle, because Raycast already shows the command name there.
When a list can have no items: add a List.EmptyView with a helpful message, because a blank list leaves users unsure what to do.
When a command has nothing to show on first use: show an empty view that explains the first step, because new users need a starting point.
When a list item shows progress or a percentage: use getProgressIcon from @raycast/utils, because it draws a native progress ring.
When list items carry no visual marker: add an icon to each item, because icons make long lists faster to scan.
When an action deletes or removes data: set its style to Action.Style.Destructive, because Raycast then shows it in red.
When an action needs one choice from several values: use ActionPanel.Submenu, because a submenu keeps the action panel short.
When a list item maps to a web page: add an Open in Browser action, because users expect to jump to the source.
When an action opens a URL: name it after what the URL shows, because a title that promises a website but opens an image confuses users.
When API data goes into HTML or markdown: escape or validate it first, because untrusted values can inject content.
When you read preferences: use the generated Preferences or ExtensionPreferences type, because a hand-written interface drifts from the manifest.
When TypeScript can not prove a value exists: check it instead of using a non-null assertion, because the ! operator hides a real undefined.
When TypeScript reports a type error: fix it or narrow the type instead of adding @ts-ignore, because the comment hides real bugs.
When ray lint warns about an unused variable: remove the variable, because the CI lint step fails on warnings.
When you finish code changes: run npm run fix-lint so Prettier formats the files, because CI rejects unformatted code.
When an exported function is not used anywhere: remove it, because dead code costs review time.
When a source file mixes constants, types and hooks: split them into single-purpose files, because small files are easier to read.
When several commands repeat the same logic: move it into one shared utility, because duplicated code drifts apart.
When a regular expression is used in a function that runs often: define it once at module level, because building it on each call wastes work.
When you change a preference: keep its name, because a new name drops the value existing users already set.
When you refactor or rename commands: keep each command's name field, because Raycast stores ranking, aliases and hotkeys under it.
When you add an option that changes output: keep the old behaviour as the default, because existing users rely on it.
When you change a dropdown preference: keep the old values valid, because users should not have to pick their setting again.
When you remove an extension or a large feature: trim it in steps, because a sudden removal leaves installed copies stuck on a stale version.
When a command needs the files selected in Finder: use getSelectedFinderItems from @raycast/api, because it avoids custom scripts.
When a required tool or setup is missing: render a Detail with the steps to fix it, because a thrown exception does not tell the user what to do.
When a list holds all its items in memory: let Raycast filter them with the built-in search, because manual filtering repeats work.
When an action only runs a function: use Action with onAction, not Action.Push, because Push is for showing a new view.
When some features need payment: say so near the top of the README, because users must know before they install.
When an extension has paid tiers: tell users in the README how to buy them, because the README is the only place to explain it.
When an extension needs an API token: list the exact token scopes in the README, because users should grant only what is needed.
When the sign-in or setup flow changes: update the README to match, because users follow the README to configure the extension.
When an extension depends on an external tool: explain in the README how to install and set it up, because users can not guess the steps.
When you add a README: keep one English README, not copies per language, because Raycast supports only US English and copies drift.
When text in an extension could be translated: write it in US English only, because Raycast does not support localization.
When the locale changes behaviour, such as units or formats: offer a preference for it, because Raycast has no localization API.
When an extension needs text generation: consider the Raycast AI API, because it reuses the user's Raycast AI access and needs no extra key.
When an extension adds AI tools: add evals to the ai section of package.json, because reviewers ask for evals on AI extensions.
When an AI extension needs guidance on when to call a tool: write it in the ai instructions field, because the model reads it with each request.
When a similar extension already exists in the Store: extend it with a PR instead of making a new one, because reviewers reject near duplicates.
When a built-in Raycast feature such as Quicklinks or File Search already does the job: do not submit an extension for it, because it adds no value.
When you change an extension you do not own: follow the contribute guide and open the PR on that extension, because the owner must sign off.
When a PR mixes fixes, refactors and new features: split it into smaller PRs, because reviewers check small changes faster.
When an extension needs native code: do not ship an .exe or other opaque binary, because reviewers treat it as an attack vector.
When an extension needs macOS native code: use the Raycast Swift tools package, because reviewers can read Swift source but not a prebuilt binary.
When an extension downloads an executable: check its hash before you run it, because a changed file could run malicious code.
When you replace a downloaded runtime: install into a new folder and swap it after success, because a failed copy would delete the working one.
When a network request can stall: pass an AbortSignal with a timeout, because a hung request blocks the command forever.
When two files hold the same version number or mapping: keep it in one shared module, because the copies drift on the next upgrade.
When a function parameter is not used: remove it, because callers will assume it changes the behaviour.
When you cache personal data such as an email address: keep it in memory unless it must persist, because LocalStorage keeps it on disk.
When code branches on an error: check its code or type, not words in its message, because message text changes between versions.
When a request is cancelled by the user: stop at once and do not retry, because a retry starts work the user cancelled.
When a sign-out clears local state: do it in a finally block, because a failed remote call must not leave stale data.
When a feature depends on a model or API version: check explicit capability data, not a name prefix, because new names break the guess.
When you write the dev script: do not make ray develop download files, because development must stay fast and work offline.
When you migrate a stored setting: write the new value back to storage, because an in-memory change is lost on the next launch.
When you integrate a web service: use its official public API, because private endpoints break without notice.
When an extension calls a third-party service: check its terms of service, because spoofed user agents or embedded app keys can break them.
When an extension shows third-party icons or images: follow their license and credit rules, because the Store can not ship content it may not redistribute.
When an extension does not need a backend: do not embed a database URL or key in it, because shipped credentials are public.
When an extension needs a large server or app: make it a documented prerequisite, because the extension should not download big releases itself.
When a command sets interval in the manifest: make it a no-view or menu-bar command, because Raycast ignores interval on view commands.
When you choose a background interval: pick the longest one that keeps the data useful, because short intervals waste battery and API quota.
When a preference controls a feature: read it everywhere that feature renders, because an ignored preference looks like a bug.
When a preference is never read by the code: remove it from the manifest, because users would change a setting that does nothing.
When an extension has several commands for one service: give the commands a subtitle with the service name, because it adds context in root search.
When you write the extension description: keep it to one short sentence about what it does, because the Store shows it in the extension list.
When commands use OAuth: wrap every command with withAccessToken, no-view ones too, because the token must be ready before the command runs.
When an extension is built on a very old template: recreate it with Create Extension and port the code, because the new template has current config.
When a review comment is not fixed yet: leave the thread unresolved, because resolved threads hide open work from the reviewer.
When you hash or read large files: use streams, not readFileSync, because a whole-file read can exhaust memory.
When a file is generated on your machine: add it to .gitignore instead of committing it, because generated files add noise to the PR.
When you reference an image from the assets folder: give only the file name, because Raycast looks in assets by default.
When a command opens a native app: use that app's icon, because a custom icon hides where the action leads.
When an icon needs a light and a dark file: pass source as an object with light and dark keys, because Raycast picks the right file per theme.
When you use a monochrome SVG icon: set a tintColor such as Color.PrimaryText, because the icon then matches the theme.
When an extension promises to hide data behind authentication: enforce the check in every view, because one unguarded view leaks the data.
When a native helper writes to a path it gets as an argument: validate the path first, because a helper with file access is a security risk.
When you add a native helper: let reviewers build it from source in the repo, because they can not verify a precompiled file.
When a PR changes a multi-step flow: attach a screencast to the PR, because reviewers want to see the flow before they try it.
When the PR checks fail: fix them before you ask for review, because reviewers wait for a passing build.
When an automated reviewer leaves comments on the PR: address them before you ask for human review, because staff review after that.
When the PR has merge conflicts: resolve them before you ask for review, because a conflicting PR can not be merged.
When a PR was moved to draft: press Ready for review after you push the fixes, because reviewers only look at PRs marked ready.
When you call a system binary whose location can vary: resolve it from PATH or check that it exists, because a hard-coded path fails on some setups.
When a menu-bar command shows a title: keep it short, because the menu bar has little room.
When a constant is already exported by another module: import it instead of redefining it, because two copies can drift.
When you write the extension description: name the actual content or service the extension covers, because users pick extensions by it.
When you fill in package.json for the Store: set license to MIT, because the Store guidelines require the MIT license.
When you prepare an extension for the Store: depend on a current @raycast/api version, because the Store asks for the up-to-date API.
When you install dependencies: use npm and not yarn or pnpm, because the Raycast CI builds and publishes with npm.
When you commit an extension: leave out yarn.lock and pnpm-lock.yaml, because CI uses only package-lock.json.
When an extension is ready for review: run npm run build and open the built extension in Raycast, because the distribution build does stricter type checks.
When you plan a new Store extension: read the Raycast Extension Guidelines first, because the review checks every submission against them.
When you write extension and command titles: follow the Apple Style Guide Title Case, because the Store naming rules are based on it.
When a title contains a name that is written in lower case, such as iOS, macOS or npm: keep its own casing, because trademarks keep their spelling.
When you title an extension: prefer a noun phrase such as Emoji Search over a verb phrase, because extension titles name a thing, not an action.
When you title an extension: avoid generic words like Converter, Images or Utils, because users must see what it does from the title.
When you title a command: leave out articles, so Create Issue not Create an Issue, because the Store guide asks for short titles.
When you title a command: do not use only the service name, such as NPM, because the title must say what the command does.
When you give a command a subtitle: use the app or service name, not a description, because the subtitle adds context and is searchable.
When a command subtitle would repeat the title: leave the subtitle out, because it adds no context.
When you export the extension icon: make it 512x512 pixels, because the Store requires that size.
When the extension has separate light and dark icons: set both in package.json as the manifest describes, because Raycast picks the icon per theme.
When an extension needs setup such as an API token: add a README.md at the extension root, because Raycast shows it as About This Extension.
When required preferences need setup steps: add a help.md at the extension root, because Raycast shows it beside the preferences form.
When you publish an extension: give it at least one category in package.json, because every Store extension needs a category.
When you set categories: use the exact Title Case names from the list, such as Developer Tools, because categories are case-sensitive.
When you add Store screenshots: add at most six and ideally three or more, because the details page shows up to six.
When you make a Store screenshot by hand: export it as a 2000 by 1250 pixel PNG, because that is the Store's size and format.
When you pick a screenshot background: choose one with good contrast to the Raycast window, because the extension must stand out.
When you choose what to capture: pick the most informative commands, because screenshots should show what the extension does in detail.
When you capture Store screenshots: use one appearance for all of them, because mixed light and dark images look inconsistent.
When you plan a significant change to someone else's extension: contact the author before you start, because big changes need the author's sign-off.
When an integration targets the same service with a different setup, such as an enterprise server: it may be a separate extension, because the setups differ.
When an extension needs a helper tool: install or set it up from the extension where possible, because extra manual downloads lose users.
When an extension downloads a binary in the background: take it from the vendor's official release and check its hash, because a swapped binary would run on users' machines.
When an extension needs a binary: do not bundle a heavy one in assets, because it grows the download for every user.
When an extension needs stored secrets: do not request Keychain access, because extensions that ask for it are rejected.
When an extension needs configuration or credentials: use the preferences API, because Raycast then handles storage and the settings form.
When a preference must be set before a command can run: mark it required, because Raycast asks for it before the command opens.
When an extension needs settings: do not build a separate command to configure it, because preferences are the place for settings.
When you title an action: use Title Case such as Copy to Clipboard, because the Store UI guidelines ask for it.
When some actions in a panel have icons: give icons to all of them, because a mix of icons and no icons looks broken.
When an action opens a submenu: end its title with an ellipsis, such as Set Priority…, because the ellipsis tells users more choices follow.
When you fill a submenu: do not repeat the parent title in each item, because Low and High read better than Set Priority Low.
When a command shows a new screen: push it with the Navigation API, because Raycast then handles back navigation like everywhere else.
When a command moves between screens: do not swap the view content by hand, because extensions with their own navigation stack are rejected.
When you set a navigationTitle on a pushed screen: keep it short, such as an issue key, because long titles get cut off.
When a screen sets navigationTitle: do not change it repeatedly on that screen, because a changing title is a sign of misuse.
When you add a text field or text area, including a preference: give it a placeholder, because placeholders show what to type.
When a list or grid has a search bar: set searchBarPlaceholder, because an empty search bar does not tell users what they can search.
When you want usage data: do not add external analytics to the extension, because the Store does not allow them.
When you write UI text: use US English spelling such as color and favorite, because Raycast supports only US English.
When a grid can have no items: add a Grid.EmptyView, because it replaces the plain No Results view with guidance.
When a list item has extra facts such as a date or count: show them as accessories, because accessories align on the right and stay scannable.
When a list accessory shows only an icon or a short value: add a tooltip, because the meaning is not always clear.
When a list item shows a time: pass a Date as the accessory, because Raycast formats it as a relative time.
When a list item shows a status: use a tag accessory with a color, because colored tags are quick to read.
When list items fall into groups: put them in List.Section with a title, because sections make long lists easier to scan.
When a list section holds a known number of items: show the count as the section subtitle, because users see the size at a glance.
When users may search an item by words that are not in its title: add them as keywords, because built-in filtering also matches keywords.
When list items can be re-ordered or reloaded: give each item a stable id, because Raycast keeps the selection by id.
When list items have long content: use isShowingDetail with List.Item.Detail, because a split view shows it without a new screen.
When a detail view shows structured facts: use Detail.Metadata labels, tags and links, because metadata renders as a clean side panel.
When a list detail panel shows key facts: use List.Item.Detail.Metadata, because it renders aligned labels under the markdown.
When a list needs a filter such as a category or account: use a searchBarAccessory dropdown, because it keeps the filter beside the search.
When a search bar dropdown should remember its choice: set storeValue, because Raycast then restores the last selection.
When the search text queries a remote API: set filtering to false and handle onSearchTextChange, because built-in filtering would hide server results.
When search text triggers network requests: set throttle on the list, because it avoids a request on every keystroke.
When the items are mainly images such as icons or photos: use Grid instead of List, because a grid shows visual content better.
When you use a Grid: set columns and aspectRatio to fit the content, because the default size may crop or shrink images.
When grid images have mixed shapes: set fit to Grid.Fit.Contain, because it shows the whole image without cropping.
When grid images touch their cell edges: set an inset, because a small inset keeps icons from looking cramped.
When a command shows rich text: render it as markdown in a Detail, because Raycast styles headings, code and images natively.
When a Detail view shows content: give it an action panel, because users expect to copy or open what they see.
When markdown shows an image in a Detail: set its size with the raycast-height or raycast-width query, because large images push text off screen.
When you add a form field: give it a title and a placeholder, because users need to know what each field expects.
When a command shows a form: add an Action.SubmitForm as the first action, because it binds to Cmd+Enter.
When a form field needs a short explanation: use its info prop, because Raycast shows it as a tooltip next to the field.
When a form needs a note above the fields: use Form.Description, because it renders as aligned text in the form.
When a form has groups of fields: separate them with Form.Separator, because visual groups make long forms clearer.
When a form field should remember its last value: set storeValue, because Raycast then pre-fills it next time.
When a form asks for a date or time: use Form.DatePicker, because it gives a native picker and a Date value.
When a form only needs a day: set the date picker type to Date, because the time part would confuse users.
When a form asks for a file or folder: use Form.FilePicker, because it opens the native file dialog.
When a form asks for a secret: use Form.PasswordField, because it hides the typed text.
When a form allows several values from a set: use Form.TagPicker, because it handles multi-select natively.
When a form dropdown has many options: group them with Form.Dropdown.Section, because grouped options are easier to scan.
When a text area takes markdown: set enableMarkdown, because Raycast then highlights the syntax.
When a form field has rules such as required input: validate it and set the field error, because users see the problem next to the field.
When a form has several validated fields: use useForm from @raycast/utils, because it wires values, errors and submit for you.
When a form field is required: use FormValidation.Required with useForm, because it gives the standard required-field message.
When a pushed form is submitted: call pop to return to the previous screen, because users expect to land back where they started.
When an action finishes the user's task: close the window with closeMainWindow or a HUD, because the user wants to move on.
When a command finishes and should reset: call popToRoot or close with popToRootType, because the next open should start fresh.
When you build an action panel: put the most common action first, because Enter runs the first action.
When an item has a second common action: put it second, because Cmd+Enter runs the second action.
When an action panel has many actions: group them in ActionPanel.Section, because groups make the panel easier to scan.
When an action panel belongs to one item: set its title to the item name, because it reminds users what they act on.
When users may want an item's text or URL: add Action.CopyToClipboard, because it copies and confirms in one step.
When the result is text the user wants in the front app: add Action.Paste, because it inserts the text where the user works.
When an item is a local file: add Action.ShowInFinder, because users often want to see the file in place.
When an item is a local file: add Action.OpenWith, because users may want a specific app for it.
When an action matches a common pattern such as delete or refresh: use Keyboard.Shortcut.Common, because it gives the shortcut users know.
When you assign shortcuts in one action panel: give each action a unique one, because a clash makes one action unreachable.
When an extension supports Windows and macOS: define shortcuts per platform, because Cmd does not exist on Windows.
When an item has a URL users revisit: add Action.CreateQuicklink, because users can then open it from root search.
When an item is reusable text: consider Action.CreateSnippet, because users can turn it into a Raycast snippet.
When an action needs a date from the user: use Action.PickDate, because it opens a native date picker in the panel.
When users may need to change a setting: add an action that calls openExtensionPreferences, because it opens the right settings page.
When a setting belongs to one command: use openCommandPreferences, because it opens that command's settings.
When a preference applies to one command only: declare it on that command, because extension-wide preferences show for every command.
When you declare a preference: pick the type that fits, such as password for tokens and checkbox for flags, because the form adapts to it.
When a preference holds an API key or token: use the password type, because Raycast then masks the value.
When a preference has a sensible default: set default in the manifest, because users can start without configuring it.
When you declare a preference: write a clear description, because Raycast shows it under the field.
When you declare a checkbox preference: give it a label, because the label is the text next to the box.
When users choose an app in settings: use the appPicker preference type, because it lists installed apps.
When a command needs one or two inputs: declare arguments in the manifest, because users can type them in root search.
When you declare a command argument: give it a placeholder, because the placeholder is the only label users see.
When a command needs more than three inputs: use a form instead of arguments, because a command can declare at most three arguments.
When an argument holds a secret: use the password argument type, because it hides the typed value.
When a command does its work without UI: set mode to no-view, because Raycast then runs it without opening a window.
When a no-view command finishes: confirm with showHUD, because the main window is closed and a HUD is the visible feedback.
When an action deletes data: ask with confirmAlert first, because users must be able to cancel a destructive step.
When a confirm alert guards a destructive step: set the primary action style to Alert.ActionStyle.Destructive, because it marks the risk in red.
When a command copies text in code: use Clipboard.copy, because it writes to the system clipboard on every platform.
When a command copies a password or token: pass the concealed option, because clipboard history then does not keep it.
When a command works on selected text: read it with getSelectedText, because it gets the selection from the front app.
When an extension must keep small data between runs: use LocalStorage from @raycast/api, because it is encrypted and scoped to the extension.
When an extension caches data for speed: use the Cache API, because it is synchronous and evicts old entries.
When different commands cache unrelated data: give each Cache a namespace, because keys from separate features must not collide.
When an extension writes files of its own: store them under environment.supportPath, because that folder belongs to the extension.
When code needs a file from assets on disk: build its path from environment.assetsPath, because the install folder differs per user.
When code must behave differently during development: check environment.isDevelopment, because it is false in the Store build.
When a command can run in the background: check environment.launchType, because user and background launches need different behaviour.
When a command uses Raycast AI: check environment.canAccess(AI) first, because not every user has AI access.
When a command calls AI.ask: pick a model only if the task needs it, because the default model follows the user's settings.
When an AI call must give precise output: set a low creativity, because higher creativity adds variation.
When you write an AI tool: document every input field with a JSDoc comment, because the model reads it to fill the input.
When an AI tool changes or deletes data: export a confirmation function, because users must approve the action first.
When you declare an AI tool in the manifest: write a description that says when to use it, because the model picks tools by it.
When an AI tool returns data: return only the fields the model needs, because large outputs waste context.
When an extension signs users in with OAuth: use the OAuth PKCE client from @raycast/api, because it keeps no client secret in the extension.
When a provider is built into @raycast/utils, such as GitHub or Linear: use OAuthService, because it already handles the flow.
When an OAuth token expires: refresh it with the stored refresh token, because users should not sign in again each time.
When a provider does not support PKCE: use the Raycast OAuth proxy, because it keeps the client secret off the device.
When code inside withAccessToken needs the token: call getAccessToken, because it returns the token the wrapper prepared.
When a menu-bar menu has groups: use MenuBarExtra.Section, because sections add separators and titles.
When a menu-bar command shows an icon: use a monochrome icon that adapts to the theme, because it must match the menu bar in light and dark.
When a menu item has a variant: use the alternate prop, because users reveal it by holding Option.
When a menu-bar command shows data that changes: set an interval, because the menu bar only updates when the command runs.
When a no-view command has a live value: show it with updateCommandMetadata, because the subtitle updates in root search.
When one command must start another command: use launchCommand, because it passes context and respects the launch type.
When a command is opened with data from another command: read it from launchContext, because it carries the passed values.
When users want a link that opens a command with arguments: use createDeeplink from @raycast/utils, because it builds a valid Raycast URL.
When a list item stands for a website: use getFavicon from @raycast/utils as its icon, because the site's own icon is familiar.
When a list item stands for a person without a photo: use getAvatarIcon from @raycast/utils, because it draws an initials avatar.
When a command runs AppleScript: use runAppleScript from @raycast/utils, because it handles timeouts and the osascript call.
When a Windows command runs PowerShell: use runPowerShellScript from @raycast/utils, because it handles the process call for you.
When an expensive async function is called often with the same input: wrap it with withCache from @raycast/utils, because results are reused.
When users pick from the same list often: sort with useFrecencySorting from @raycast/utils, because frequent and recent items rise to the top.
When an action or item needs a generic symbol: use the built-in Icon set, because those icons match Raycast's style.
When you tint icons or tags: use the Color constants, because they adapt to light and dark themes.
When you show a remote avatar image: set mask to Image.Mask.Circle, because round avatars match the Raycast style.
When an icon loads from a URL: set a fallback icon, because remote images can fail or load slowly.
When a list item is a local file: use fileIcon with the path, because Raycast shows the file's system icon.
When a command moves or resizes windows: use the WindowManagement API, because it works with Raycast's own window handling.
When a command opens a file or URL in an app: use open from @raycast/api, because it handles the app and path for you.
When a command needs installed apps: use getApplications, because it returns names, paths and bundle IDs.
When a command deletes user files: move them with trash from @raycast/api, because users can then restore them.
When code must reveal a file after creating it: call showInFinder, because it opens Finder at the file.
When a command needs the content of the open browser tab: use the BrowserExtension API, because it reads the tab through the Raycast browser extension.
When you lay out an extension: put source in src, images in assets and Store images in metadata, because Raycast and the Store expect that layout.
When you add a command to the manifest: create a file in src with the same name as the command, because Raycast loads the command from it.
When an extension needs credentials: never hard-code them in the source, because the source of every Store extension is public.
When an AI tool returns an empty or failed result: return a clear message to the model, because it can then explain or try another way.
When you write AI evals: give each eval an input and expected tool calls, because the eval runner checks which tools the model used.
When users may search for a command by other words: add keywords to the command in the manifest, because root search matches them.
When a command is optional for most users: set disabledByDefault, because users can enable it without clutter in root search.
When you declare a command: write a one-sentence description, because the Store and preferences show it.
When you set up tsconfig.json: keep strict mode on, because strict checks catch null and type bugs before users hit them.
When you type a value from outside, such as an API response: use unknown or a real type instead of any, because any turns off type checking.
When code reads a JSON API response: declare an interface for the fields it uses, because typed fields catch renamed or missing keys.
When a value has type unknown: narrow it with a type guard before use, because unchecked casts hide wrong shapes.
When a value does not match the type you want: fix the type or narrow it, not cast with as, because casts silence real mismatches.
When a value can only be one of a few strings: type it as a union of string literals, because the compiler then rejects typos.
When a switch covers a union type: add a never check in the default branch, because a new member then fails to compile.
When you define a constant list or map: mark it as const, because literal types and readonly keep it from changing.
When an import is used only as a type: use import type, because the import is then removed from the bundle.
When you read a property that may be missing: use optional chaining, because it avoids a crash on undefined.
When you give a default for a missing value: use ?? instead of ||, because || also replaces valid values like 0 and empty strings.
When a variable is never reassigned: declare it with const, because const shows the value does not change.
When you declare a variable: use const or let, never var, because var has function scope and hoisting surprises.
When you compare values: use === and !==, because loose equality converts types in surprising ways.
When you write asynchronous code: use async and await instead of long then chains, because the flow is easier to read.
When you call an async function: await it or handle its rejection, because an unhandled promise fails silently.
When several independent async calls are needed: run them with Promise.all, because sequential awaits add up the wait time.
When a loop awaits independent work on each pass: collect the promises and await them together, because awaiting in the loop runs them one by one.
When a Node API offers a promise version: use it, such as fs/promises, because callbacks mix badly with async code.
When code runs during a React render: do not call synchronous file system functions, because they block the UI thread.
When you run a shell program with user input: use execFile with an argument array, because exec with a joined string allows command injection.
When you must build a shell command string: escape every user value, because unescaped input can run other commands.
When you build file paths: use path.join or path.resolve, because hand-joined strings break on separators and other platforms.
When a path starts at the home folder: expand it with os.homedir, because Node does not expand the tilde.
When you build a URL with query values: use URL and URLSearchParams, because they encode special characters correctly.
When you put user text into a URL path: encode it with encodeURIComponent, because spaces and slashes break the URL.
When you format dates for display: use Intl.DateTimeFormat or a small date library, because hand-built formats are error-prone.
When you show numbers, money or units: format them with Intl.NumberFormat, because it adds separators and currency symbols correctly.
When you persist a date: store it as an ISO 8601 string or timestamp, because Date objects do not survive JSON as dates.
When you change arrays or objects held in React state: create new copies, because mutating them in place skips re-renders.
When you render a list of elements: use a stable unique key such as an id, not the array index, because index keys break item identity.
When a value can be computed from props or state: compute it during render, because duplicated state gets out of sync.
When a render does an expensive calculation: wrap it in useMemo, because it then runs only when its inputs change.
When a callback is passed to a memoized child: wrap it in useCallback, because a new function each render defeats the memo.
When a command component grows long: split it into smaller components, because small components are easier to read and reuse.
When several components share stateful logic: extract it into a custom hook, because one hook keeps the logic in one place.
When you call React hooks: call them at the top level of a component and never inside conditions, because hook order must not change.
When you write a React component: keep the render function free of side effects, because React may render more than once.
When a value changes what is shown: keep it in state, not in a ref, because changing a ref does not re-render.
When you render conditionally with &&: make the left side a boolean, because a 0 would render as text.
When you name a React component: use PascalCase, because JSX treats lower-case names as built-in tags.
When a component takes props: declare a props type, because typed props catch missing or wrong values.
When a module exports helpers: use named exports, because they keep import names consistent and searchable.
When you write a command file: default-export the command function, because Raycast loads the command from the default export.
When a function has guard conditions: return early, because deep nesting is hard to follow.
When you name variables and functions: use full descriptive words, because short cryptic names slow down reviewers.
When you name variables and functions in TypeScript: use camelCase, because it is the common TypeScript style.
When a module-level constant never changes: name it in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, because readers then see it is a fixed value.
When code uses a number with a special meaning: give it a named constant, because a bare number hides its purpose.
When code is no longer needed: delete it instead of commenting it out, because git keeps the history.
When an import is no longer used: remove it, because unused imports add noise and can grow the bundle.
When a condition can never be true: remove the branch, because dead branches confuse readers.
When you add a dependency: use a caret range on a stable major version, because it takes fixes without breaking changes.
When a dependency adds only one small helper: write the helper instead, because each dependency adds size and risk.
When npm warns that a package is deprecated: replace it, because deprecated packages stop getting security fixes.
When you add or update dependencies: check npm audit for known vulnerabilities, because the extension runs on users' machines.
When a package is used only for build or lint tooling: put it in devDependencies, because it is not needed at runtime.
When an extension calls a web API: use HTTPS URLs, because plain HTTP exposes tokens and data in transit.
When you send an API token: put it in a request header, not in the URL, because URLs end up in history and server records.
When an API returns 429: wait for the Retry-After time before the next call, because ignoring rate limits can get the key blocked.
When code compares or displays dates: account for the user's time zone, because UTC and local dates differ near midnight.
When you sort strings shown to users: use localeCompare, because plain comparison sorts accents and case wrongly.
When you sort an array you did not create: sort a copy, because sort changes the array in place.
When you remove items while you iterate: build a new filtered array, because splicing during iteration skips items.
When code looks up items by key many times: build a Map once, because repeated find calls are slow on long lists.
When you remove duplicate values: use a Set, because it is clearer and faster than nested loops.
When you combine strings with values: use template literals, because they are easier to read than concatenation.
When code throws: throw an Error instance, not a string, because Error objects keep a stack trace.
When you rethrow an error with more context: pass the original as cause, because the root cause stays visible.
When typing triggers expensive local work: debounce it, because work on every keystroke makes the UI lag.
When code processes a large data set: process it in chunks or a worker, because a long loop freezes the command.
When you format code: keep the Prettier config the template ships, because consistent formatting keeps diffs small.
When a regular expression is complex: give it a named constant and use named groups, because readers can then follow it.
When you build a regular expression from user text: escape special characters, because input like a dot or bracket changes the match.
When a list item needs secondary text: put it in subtitle, not in the title, because the title stays short and easy to scan.
When an action opens a new screen: use Action.Push with a target view, because it pushes onto the Raycast navigation stack.
When code must set or clear the search text: pass searchText together with onSearchTextChange, because a controlled search bar stays in sync.
When a form edits an existing item: pre-fill the fields with defaultValue or initialValues, because users then change values instead of retyping.
When a list item is a local file: set its quickLook prop and add Action.ToggleQuickLook, because users can then preview it with Quick Look.
When an extension reads another app's SQLite database: open it read-only or query a copy, because writing could corrupt the other app's data.
When user text goes into an AppleScript string: escape quotes and backslashes, because unescaped input breaks or changes the script.
When a long switch or if chain maps fixed keys to values: use an object or Map lookup, because a table is shorter and easier to extend.
When a helper inside a component uses no props or state: move it outside the component, because it is then not re-created on each render.
